The last two rows are linked. A unit test has fixed inputs, so its result in production would always be the same as in CI. Running it again in every production job only costs money. A data test, on the contrary, must run in production, because the data changes every day.
Unit tests do not look at your data
(trap T126). They never read the real rows of the input tables, and they cannot find order 159 or a duplicated id in the warehouse. Their job is to prove that the
is right for the cases you thought of. An exam answer like "add a unit test to detect duplicates in the raw orders table" is wrong: that is a data test.
Unit tests live in a YAML file inside
: that folder is for data tests. Here is the complete list of keys:

blocks.text:
unit_tests:
  - name: <unique name of the test>
    description: <optional text>
    model: <the model to test>
    versions:                    # optional, for versioned models
      include: [<versions>]      # or exclude: [<versions>]
    config:                      # optional
      tags: <string or list>
      meta: {...}
      enabled: true | false      # default true
    given:                       # one entry per ref() / source() of the model
      - input: ref('<model or seed>') | source('<source>', '<table>') | this
        format: dict | csv | sql # default dict
        rows: <the rows>         # or fixture: <file name in tests/fixtures/>
    expect:
      format: dict | csv | sql   # default dict
      rows: <the expected rows>  # or fixture: <file name>
    overrides:                   # optional
      macros: {is_incremental: true, ...}
      vars: {...}
      env_vars: {...}

blocks.text:
- name: test_fct_orders_incremental_keeps_only_new_rows
    description: In an incremental run, only orders loaded after the newest loaded_at already in the table are processed.
    model: fct_orders
    overrides:
      macros:
        is_incremental: true
    given:
      - input: ref('int_orders__enriched')
        rows:
          - {order_id: 1, customer_id: 1, order_date: 2025-12-30, status: shipped, loaded_at: "2025-12-30 10:00:00", paid_amount: 10.00}
          - {order_id: 2, customer_id: 2, order_date: 2025-12-31, status: placed, loaded_at: "2026-01-02 07:00:00", paid_amount: 25.00}
          - {order_id: 3, customer_id: 1, order_date: 2026-01-01, status: completed, loaded_at: "2026-01-01 08:00:00", paid_amount: 6.00}
      - input: ref('int_orders__payment_methods_pivoted')
        rows:
          - {order_id: 2, bank_transfer_amount: 0, coupon_amount: 5.00, credit_card_amount: 20.00, gift_card_amount: 0}
          - {order_id: 3, bank_transfer_amount: 0, coupon_amount: 0, credit_card_amount: 6.00, gift_card_amount: 0}
      # 'this' = the current content of the incremental table
      - input: this
        rows:
          - {order_id: 1, loaded_at: "2025-12-31 00:00:00"}
    expect:
      rows:
        - {order_id: 2, status: placed, coupon_amount: 5.00, credit_card_amount: 20.00, amount: 25.00}
        - {order_id: 3, status: completed, coupon_amount: 0, credit_card_amount: 6.00, amount: 6.00}

  - name: test_fct_orders_full_refresh_keeps_all_rows
    description: In a full refresh (is_incremental false), every order is processed.
    model: fct_orders
    overrides:
      macros:
        is_incremental: false
    given:
      - input: ref('int_orders__enriched')
        rows:
          - {order_id: 1, loaded_at: "2025-12-30 10:00:00", paid_amount: 10.00}
          - {order_id: 2, loaded_at: "2026-01-02 07:00:00", paid_amount: 25.00}
      - input: ref('int_orders__payment_methods_pivoted')
        rows: []
    expect:
      rows:
        - {order_id: 1, amount: 10.00, credit_card_amount: 0}
        - {order_id: 2, amount: 25.00, credit_card_amount: 0}
